title: Sets, Relations and Propositional Logic
objectives: Use set notation (union, intersection, complement, subset) and compute cardinalities with inclusion-exclusion
Decide whether a relation is reflexive, symmetric or transitive, and recognise equivalence relations
Evaluate compound propositions from truth tables and state when an implication is false
Apply De Morgan's laws to negate compound conditions correctly
motivation: Every screening rule a desk runs - 'reject orders larger than 500 and prices outside the band', 'these two funds must not share more than three names' - is set membership and propositional logic wearing a company badge. Getting the logic wrong does not crash anything: the filter silently accepts or rejects the wrong orders. This lesson gives you the exact vocabulary so later graph, probability and algorithm material has something precise to stand on.

blocks.md: A **set** is a collection of distinct elements with no order and no duplicates: $A = \{\text{AAPL}, \text{MSFT}, \text{TSLA}\}$ and $B = \{\text{MSFT}, \text{XOM}\}$ are two watchlists. We write $x \in A$ when $x$ is a member, $A \subseteq B$ when every member of $A$ is also a member of $B$, and $|A|$ for the **cardinality** (size). Three operations do nearly all the work: the **union** $A \cup B$ holds elements in either set, the **intersection** $A \cap B$ holds elements in both, and the **complement** $U \setminus A$ holds universe elements missing from $A$. Here, if the universe is $U = \{\text{AAPL}, \text{MSFT}, \text{TSLA}, \text{XOM}, \text{JPM}, \text{BAC}\}$, then $A \cup B = \{\text{AAPL}, \text{MSFT}, \text{TSLA}, \text{XOM}\}$ and $U \setminus A = \{\text{XOM}, \text{JPM}, \text{BAC}\}$.

Counting a union naively as $|A| + |B|$ double-counts the overlap. The **inclusion-exclusion** identity fixes it: $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B| = 3 + 2 - 1 = 4$, since MSFT sits in both lists. This one-line check catches a surprising number of production bugs: any code that builds a combined list by appending two lists and then counting length without de-duplicating has quietly violated exactly this identity.

blocks.title: Overlap audits are set arithmetic
blocks.md: When compliance asks how many distinct names two funds hold together, the answer is $|A \cup B|$, not $|A| + |B|$. A fund holding 120 names and another holding 80 with 25 shared names hold $120 + 80 - 25 = 175$ distinct instruments - and that intersection count is precisely what concentration limits measure.

blocks.caption: In code, a set is a hash table: membership tests jump straight to one bucket. Notice 15 and 7 land in the same bucket - real implementations pay for that collision with chaining or probing.

blocks.md: A **relation** from $A$ to $B$ is just a set of ordered pairs - for example 'this venue quotes this instrument'. A relation on a single set (pairs where both sides come from the same set) is classified by three properties. **Reflexive**: every element relates to itself, so $(x,x)$ is present for all $x$. **Symmetric**: whenever $(x,y)$ is present, so is $(y,x)$. **Transitive**: whenever $(x,y)$ and $(y,z)$ are present, $(x,z)$ must be too. Take $R = \{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2)\}$ on $\{1,2,3\}$: all three diagonal pairs make it reflexive; $(1,2)$ is present but $(2,1)$ is not, so it is not symmetric; and the only nontrivial chain, $(1,1)$ then $(1,2)$, already has its required conclusion $(1,2)$, so it is transitive.

A relation with **all three** properties is an **equivalence relation**: it carves its set into disjoint **equivalence classes** that behave like 'same category' buckets - same remainder class, same risk bucket, same settlement currency. Disjointness of the classes is what makes equivalence relations the backbone of partitioning problems, including the union-find structures you will meet in the algorithms phase.

A **proposition** is a statement that is definitely true or false: 'the order size exceeds 500' is one; 'the order is large' is not, until you define large. Compound statements are built with $\neg$ (not), $\land$ (and), $\lor$ (or) and $\rightarrow$ (implies), and every combination's truth is pinned down by a truth table. The only row of $p \rightarrow q$ worth memorising is the one people get wrong: the implication is **false exactly when $p$ is true and $q$ is false**. An implication with a false premise is vacuously true - 'if the market is closed then the spread is zero' is not a lie just because the market is open.

Two consequences of that table carry most practical weight. First, the **contrapositive**: $p \rightarrow q$ is logically identical to $\neg q \rightarrow \neg p$, so 'if the order filled, the price crossed the limit' says the same thing as 'if the price never crossed the limit, the order did not fill'. Second, **De Morgan's laws** tell you how negation flips connectives:

blocks.tex:
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q, \qquad 
eg(p \lor q) \equiv 
eg p \land 
eg q
blocks.caption: Negating an AND gives an OR of negations, and vice versa.

blocks.title: Worked example: negating a trading rule
items: Rule: raise an alert when $p$ = 'spread widened' AND $q$ = 'volume exceeded 1M'. Alert condition: $p \land q$.
The rule fails to fire exactly when $\neg(p \land q)$ holds.
By De Morgan: $\neg p \lor \neg q$ - 'the spread did not widen OR the volume did not exceed 1M'.
Check one row: spread widened (T), volume 800k (so $q$ is F): $p \land q$ = F, alert silent. $\neg p \lor \neg q$ = F $\lor$ T = T. Consistent.
The wrong 'negation' $\neg p \land \neg q$ (spread stable AND volume low) would miss rows like this one - a silently broken risk check.

blocks.code:
import itertools
for p, q in itertools.product([True, False], repeat=2):
    print(p, q, not (p and q), (not p) or (not q), (not p) or q)
# Columns 3 and 4 match on every row: De Morgan verified.
# Column 5 is p -> q: false only in row (True, False).
blocks.caption: Logic is checkable: enumerate all rows and compare.

blocks.title: Or is inclusive in logic
blocks.md: $p \lor q$ is true when both sides are true - unlike the everyday 'or' that suggests one or the other. Code that implements 'reject if the price is stale or the size exceeds limits' must reject when **both** conditions hold too. The XOR of everyday speech has to be built deliberately, not assumed.

guidedExercise.prompt: Let the universe be $U = \{1,2,\dots,10\}$, $A$ = the even numbers in $U$, and $B$ = the multiples of 3 in $U$. (1) List $A \cup B$ and $A \cap B$ and confirm inclusion-exclusion on the sizes. (2) List $U \setminus (A \cap B)$ and $(U \setminus A) \cup (U \setminus B)$ and confirm De Morgan's law numerically. (3) In words, what condition does $U \setminus (A \cap B)$ describe?
hints: $A = \{2,4,6,8,10\}$ and $B = \{3,6,9\}$ - which number sits in both?
De Morgan for sets: the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements.
guidedExercise.solution: (1) $A \cup B = \{2,3,4,6,8,9,10\}$, $|A \cup B| = 7$; $A \cap B = \{6\}$; check: $5 + 3 - 1 = 7$. (2) $U \setminus (A \cap B) = U \setminus \{6\} = \{1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10\}$. Meanwhile $U \setminus A = \{1,3,5,7,9\}$ and $U \setminus B = \{1,2,4,5,7,8,10\}$, whose union is $\{1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10\}$ - identical, as De Morgan promises. (3) It describes: not (even AND a multiple of 3), i.e. every number that fails to be both even and divisible by 3.

independentExercise.prompt: (1) On $\{a,b,c\}$ consider $R = \{(a,a),(b,b),(c,c),(a,b),(b,c)\}$. Which of reflexive, symmetric, transitive hold, and which fail? Name the specific pair(s) that break each failing property. (2) Would adding $(a,c)$ and $(b,a)$ and $(c,b)$ make $R$ an equivalence relation? (3) State the contrapositive of: 'if the order is filled, then the price crossed the limit.'
hints: For transitivity, hunt for chains $(x,y),(y,z)$ whose shortcut $(x,z)$ is missing.
An equivalence relation also needs the classes to close up - symmetric pairs must come in both directions.
independentExercise.solution: (1) Reflexive holds (all three diagonal pairs). Symmetric fails: $(a,b) \in R$ but $(b,a) \notin R$ (likewise $(b,c)$ without $(c,b)$). Transitive fails: $(a,b)$ and $(b,c)$ are present but $(a,c)$ is not. (2) No. Adding $(a,c)$, $(b,a)$, $(c,b)$ repairs some holes but $(c,a)$ is still missing: symmetry breaks because $(a,c) \in R'$ while $(c,a) \notin R'$, and transitivity breaks on the chain $(c,b),(b,a)$ which demands the missing $(c,a)$. The relation becomes an equivalence relation only once $(c,a)$ is added too, collapsing everything into the single class $\{a,b,c\}$. (3) Contrapositive: 'if the price did not cross the limit, then the order was not filled.'

commonMistakes: Counting $|A \cup B|$ as $|A| + |B|$ and double-counting the intersection - inclusion-exclusion subtracts $|A \cap B|$.
Writing the negation of $p \land q$ as $\neg p \land \neg q$; De Morgan forces an OR between the negated pieces.
Treating $p \rightarrow q$ as claiming causation or claiming the converse; it is only false when $p$ is true and $q$ is false.
Assuming a relation with all diagonal pairs is automatically symmetric or transitive - the off-diagonal pairs decide.
realWorldApplication: Set operations drive de-duplicated reporting, permissions checks (is this user in the allowed group?) and compliance overlap counts; propositional logic is the semantics behind every boolean filter, feature flag and alert condition in production code.
quantFinanceApplication: Position limits, concentration rules and kill-switch conditions are compound propositions evaluated on every order; a De Morgan slip in one clause can silence a risk alert exactly when both risk conditions occur - the scenario the rule was written for.
summary: Sets have no order or duplicates; $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|$ prevents double-counting shared elements.
Relations are sets of pairs; reflexive + symmetric + transitive = equivalence relation, which partitions the set into disjoint classes.
$p \rightarrow q$ is false exactly when $p$ is true and $q$ is false; its contrapositive $\neg q \rightarrow \neg p$ is logically equivalent.
De Morgan: negating $\land$ yields $\lor$ of negations and vice versa - the single most-used identity in writing correct boolean conditions.

quiz.prompt: Two portfolios hold $|A| = 12$ and $|B| = 7$ instruments with $|A \cap B| = 3$ shared names. How many distinct instruments do they hold in total?
quiz.explanation: $|A \cup B| = 12 + 7 - 3 = 16$. Choice 19 double-counts the 3 shared names; inclusion-exclusion subtracts them once.

quiz.prompt: Sets $A$ and $B$ satisfy $|A| = 4$ and $|B| = 3$. How many ordered pairs are in the Cartesian product $A \times B$?
quiz.explanation: Each of the 4 elements of $A$ pairs with each of the 3 elements of $B$: $4 \times 3 = 12$ ordered pairs.

quiz.prompt: On the integers, consider the relation $x \neq y$ (not equal). Which property does it satisfy?
quiz.explanation:
Symmetric holds ($x 
eq y$ implies $y 
eq x$). Reflexive fails ($x 
eq x$ is false), and transitive fails: $1 
eq 2$, $2 
eq 3$, but $1 = 3$.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
p, q = True, False
print(not (p or q))
print((not p) and (not q))
print((not p) or q)
quiz.explanation:
The first two lines are De Morgan's pair $
eg(p \lor q)$ and $
eg p \land 
eg q$, which must match - both False here. The third is $p ightarrow q$, false exactly because $p$ is true and $q$ is false.

quiz.prompt: A desk rule says: 'if the spread widens beyond 20 bps, then the position is hedged.' On which day is this rule VIOLATED?
options: Spread widened beyond 20 bps and the position is hedged
Spread widened beyond 20 bps and the position is not hedged
Spread stayed narrow and the position is not hedged
Spread stayed narrow and the position is hedged
quiz.explanation: An implication is false only when the premise holds and the conclusion fails: spread widened (true) and not hedged (false). Narrow-spread days are vacuously fine either way.

quiz.prompt: State the contrapositive of: 'If the trade is profitable, then the position was held to expiry.'
quiz.modelAnswer: If the position was not held to expiry, then the trade is not profitable.
quiz.explanation: Contrapositive of $p \rightarrow q$ is $\neg q \rightarrow \neg p$: negate both sides and swap them. It is logically equivalent to the original statement.

flashcards.front: When is an implication $p \rightarrow q$ false?
flashcards.back: Only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false; if $p$ is false the implication is vacuously true. Equivalent to its contrapositive $\neg q \rightarrow \neg p$.
